content.text: # creating-views Skill # Creating Views A view is one self-contained HTML page that the Amp web UI renders inline in your reply, in a sandboxed frame on the thread's own background that follows the reader's light or dark theme. Publish the page as a visual artifact, then embed it in your reply with Markdown image syntax: 1. Call the `artifact` tool with `action: "publish"`, `kind: "visual"`, `folder: "visuals"`, a short title, and the whole page as `content`. The content is HTML and nothing else: no Markdown and no code fence around it. 2. Put the returned `url` in your reply as an image, on its own line: `![Deep mode growth](URL)`. The reader sees the page there, and can open it as an artifact they can share. To show the view inside a document artifact, such as a report, put the same image line in the document's Markdown. ````markdown Deep mode is now Amp's second most used mode. ![Deep mode tripled in six weeks](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/deep-mode-growth-…) Most of the growth came from existing Smart users switching, not new users. ```` To change a view, publish the same artifact again with `edits` or new `content` and embed it again. Each publish replaces the page, so every embed of it shows the latest revision; publish a new artifact when the reader should keep the earlier version. Without the `artifact` tool, write the page in a fenced code block with the `amp-view` language tag instead, which renders the same way. The reader sees the view in place. Do not announce it or restate it in your text; write only what the view does not say. ## When to use a view Use a view when seeing answers the question faster than reading: - Data: a trend over time, a ranking, a distribution, or a comparison across more than about six values. - Systems: any diagram, such as an architecture, flowchart, sequence, state machine, timeline, race between callers, tree, or commit graph, including small static ones. - Derivations: how a number is computed, with inputs the reader can change. - Design: a quick UI experiment, such as a component or screen mockup, an interaction prototype, a layout wireframe, or two or three design directions side by side. - Any request to chart, plot, graph, visualize, diagram, mock up, prototype, sketch, try out a UI idea, or build a dashboard. Use Markdown instead for a short list, a table of a few rows, or one or two numbers. A view adds nothing to a code change summary; show the diff instead. ## The standard A view must look like it shipped with Amp: calm, quiet, and precise. Readers glance at it between other work, so it has one point, and that point is legible in one second. Everything else is gray and small so that one thing stands out. Restraint is the style: when in doubt, remove. Looking right is the easy part. Views fail far more often because the chart does not show what the title claims, so every view must also prove its point: - Before writing code, write the one sentence the reader should take away. For a chart it becomes the title; for a mockup or diagram it decides which state to open on. - Compute every number in the title from the data embedded in the view. Never quote a number the view does not contain, and never let a title rest on a default or placeholder value; in a calculator, generate the title from the current state. - Choose the encoding the claim needs. A claim about a multiple plots the multiple, a claim about a share draws the share, and "N% within X" draws a cumulative share. `reference/charts.md` covers this. - Make the default state show the point at 360px without any interaction. Open a stepper on the step that proves the title, color the path that matters before anyone clicks, and open a mockup on the state that decides the design. Screenshots, phones, and skimming readers only ever see the default state. - Say in a muted subtitle or caption what was measured, over what scope, and how the measure could mislead (a partial week, a known bias in the source, an assumption). ## How to build one 1. Write the takeaway sentence. 2. Read the reference for the kind of view, in this skill's `reference/` directory: - `charts.md` for charts, distributions, calculations, comparison and decision matrices, tables, and dashboards. - `ui-explorations.md` for mockups, prototypes, design options, interactive experiments, and wireframes. - `diagrams.md` for architecture diagrams, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, state machines, timelines, race timelines, trees, commit graphs, and step-through explainers. 3. Start from the closest example in `examples/`. Each is a complete view that follows this guide; reuse its structure and code, and replace its placeholder subject and data with yours. - `indexed-lines.html`: a line chart whose title states a multiple, plotted against each series' own baseline. - `highlighted-bars.html`: a ranking with one highlighted bar, a gray tail row, and shares at the bar ends. - `cumulative-share.html`: a hand-drawn distribution (cumulative share on a log axis) with a pointer and keyboard readout. - `calculation.html`: a derivation ledger, one term per row, with inputs to change, a computed title, and the marginal cost. - `decision-matrix.html`: a weighted decision with sliders, a title computed from state, and the smallest change that flips the pick. - `design-options.html`: a UI exploration with today's behavior as a baseline, three directions, a stress condition, and working actions. - `flowchart.html`: a flowchart or state diagram that colors the path the title is about and reflows from a row to a column on phones. - `sequence.html`: a sequence diagram with a synced ledger of who holds what after each step. - `race-timeline.html`: a timeline of two concurrent callers on one time axis, with the moment the race breaks marked and the fix behind a switch. - `tree.html`: a file tree as an indented outline that opens only the path to the files the title names, with WAI-ARIA tree keys. ## The frame - The view is as wide as the reply column: about 720px on desktop and 360px on phones. Design for both. - Its height fits the document, so the whole view shows in the reply without scrolling inside it, and the reader can open it full screen. Aim for under 600px; past that, cut or split it into two views. Never size anything from the frame's height (`vh` units, `height: 100%` on `html` or `body`): the frame grows to fit the page, so such a page keeps growing. - There is no network: every request is blocked. Inline all CSS, JS, images (as data URLs), and data. Chart libraries and web fonts cannot load. - There are no popups, storage, or form submission. Clicks on `http(s)` links ask the reader first. Hover, clicks, and keys work inside the frame. Nothing can draw outside it. - Print and download buttons work. `window.print()`, called from a click or key press, prints a copy of the page as it is then, on a light background; hide controls under `@media print`. The print dialog is the only way to save a PDF. For other files, use `ui.download`. - Keep the page under 100 KB; aggregate data before embedding it. - Wrap your script in a block (`{ … }`). Top-level `const top`, `name`, or `status` collide with browser globals and stop the script. ## Tokens Amp sets these on `:root`. They update live when the reader switches theme. It does not restyle `a`, `b`, `strong`, or `h1` to `h4`, which render as browser blue links, bold, and large headings; use the kit's text classes instead of these elements. ## The kit Every view loads Amp's view kit: Amp's own components as CSS classes, Lucide icons, and `window.ui` for charts and motion. Build with it first; write your own CSS only for what it lacks. It is what makes a view look like Amp instead of a generic web page. Text and layout: - `.ui-header` wraps `.ui-title` (13px, 500) and `.ui-sub` (12px muted) with 16px below. content.text:
I made three variations of Reading room. They keep the earth tones, serif type and humanist feel, but they're each more like app UI than the first version.

![Reading room variations](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/visuals/reading-room-variations-0b245fa8-fe57-4de5-9984-173befe7f7fb)

**What made the first version feel like print:** small caps for authors, italic metadata, the drop cap, underlined search inputs, 4px corners and large serif page titles. All three variations replace these with app patterns:
- humanist sans for controls and metadata (Source Sans 3)
- boxed inputs and 6px corners
- a filled background on the active nav item
- a progress bar
- a plain label and value list for metadata

**The variations differ in where the serif goes:**
1. **Serif headings:** serif for the wordmark, page headings and the title on the book page. Everything you scan or click is sans. It reads as an app with a warm voice.
2. **Serif titles:** serif for the books themselves, meaning every title and description, in the grid and on the book page. The app around them is all sans. This is the clearest rule: serif means book content, sans means interface.
3. **App shell:** serif only on the wordmark and the book page title, with a warm sidebar for Library, Authors and Series (those routes already exist). It's the most like software and the least bookish.

**I recommend Serif titles.** It keeps most of the Reading room feel, and the rule is simple for anyone building new screens to follow.

The mockup also has an accent switcher with oxblood, terracotta and moss, plus light and dark. The earlier version is included for comparison.

**Verdict: Partially met.**

**Matches expectations:**
- Warm cream/off-white background throughout the page.
- Serif "Bookserve" wordmark, top-left of header.
- Serif "Library" heading, large, below the nav.
- Active nav item "Library" has a filled light gray/tan background (nav bar, top-left area), distinguishing it from "Market" and "Settings," which are unstyled text.
- Moss/dark green "Upload" button with an upload icon, top-right of the header row (next to "Scan library").

**Does not match expectations — cloth-bound covers:**
Only 2 of the 11 visible covers resemble the described "cloth-bound" style with a thin gold border and serif title printed on the cover: **"Meditations"** (maroon, top row, far right) and **"The Time Machine"** (brown, bottom row, far right). Both show a thin gold inset border and centered serif title/author text, consistent with the objective.

The remaining 9 covers (The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, The Communist Manifesto, Emma, Frankenstein, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Moby-Dick, Pride and Prejudice, The Sign of the Four, A Study in Scarlet) are plain flat-color rectangles (gold, red, blue, dark green, green, navy, pink/rose, slate, dark red) with **no border, no texture, and no title text on the cover itself** — the title and author only appear as plain sans-serif text below the cover block, not serif text on the cover.

- Inconsistent cover treatment: most placeholders are solid-color blocks with no visible title/border, while only two follow the intended "cloth-bound" design. This looks like an incomplete rollout of the cover style rather than a deliberate variation.
- Titles/authors below the plain-color covers use a sans-serif font, not serif, inconsistent with the serif styling implied for the design system (though this may be intentional for captions vs. in-cover text).
- No major layout defects (no clipping, overlap, or misalignment observed) in the grid, header, or search/scan/upload cluster.

**Verdict: Met.** All three expectations are satisfied.

- **Serif title:** "Sign in" at top-left of the card (~x740, y455) is rendered in a bold serif typeface.
- **Warm background:** Both the page background and card background use a warm off-white/cream tone.
- **Moss button:** The "Sign in" submit button at the bottom of the card (~x740-1260, y760-810) is a muted moss/olive green with white centered label text.

**Additional observations (not requested, but visible near areas of interest):**
- The Username field has a thick green focus ring/border, while the Password field below it has a plain gray border — inconsistent focus-state styling between the two inputs.
- No visible cursor/focus indicator issue beyond that; layout, spacing, and alignment of labels and fields are consistent and not clipped or overlapping.

Serif headings with the Moss palette is now the app's design. It's committed locally as [`0d127ac`](amp-changes:commit/0d127ac) and not pushed yet.

:::gallery side-by-side
![Library](https://ampcode.com/user-content/attachments/399a71089df0374e78b63e47cd0f8c3975106bc05427bf01f357ecb880e94045-library.png#amp-media-source=file%3A%2F%2F%2Fhome%2Fuser%2Fworkspace%2Frepo%2F.amp%2Fin%2Fartifacts%2Flibrary.png&amp-media-width=2560&amp-media-height=1600&REDACTED)

:::

**What changed:**
- **Theme tokens** in `src/styles.css`: warm paper background, brown text, Moss primary, and 6px corners, with light and dark versions. Every shadcn component picks these up automatically.
- **Fonts:** Source Sans 3 for the interface. Source Serif 4 for every `h1`, `h2` and card title, set by one base CSS rule, so page code didn't need changing. The one exception is the Market breadcrumb: it's an `h2` but sits in navigation, so I set it back to sans.
- **Top bar:** serif "Bookserve" wordmark, and the active tab now has a filled background instead of bold text.
- **Cover placeholder:** books without a cover image now get the cloth-bound look.

**One thing to approve:** the fonts are two new dependencies, `@fontsource-variable/source-serif-4` and `source-sans-3`. They're plain CSS and font files built into the image, so nothing loads from the network and there's no native code to worry about for the arm64 build.

**Checks:** I checked the Library, book, Settings and sign-in pages in the browser, and the browser confirmed both fonts loaded. `pnpm lint` is clean, Prettier passes on the changed files, and `pnpm build` succeeds with the font files in `.output/public/assets`.

**Dark mode:** the dark tokens are written, but the app has nothing that turns dark mode on yet. Light is the only theme you'll see until a toggle or system-theme switch is added.
